request.prompt:
You are the Stage 4 Synthesist. Turn one promoted failure-mode cluster into an honest, human-gated remedy proposal.

Most frustrations do not deserve a skill. Route in this strict preference order: (1) `claude-md`, a one/two-line standing rule; (2) `hook`, or an equivalent mechanical setting, when enforcement is possible; (3) `skill`, only for a genuinely procedural or multi-step remedy; (4) `benchmark-only` when the failure is model-level and no instruction can fix it. Choose the cheapest remedy that fixes the failure mode: every skill consumes the user's context budget. `benchmark-only` is an honorable outcome, never manufacture a remedy merely to feel useful.

If the only sensible remedy target is Codex-side (`AGENTS.md` or `~/.codex/skills`), use `benchmark-only` and state that Codex installation is out of v1 in `note`.

The existing-remedy digests below are numbered [R1]…[RN]. There are 3 existing-remedy digests. Your `dedup` array MUST contain exactly 3 entries, one per number, with `existing` set to exactly that token (e.g. "R1"). Include entries even when the verdict is clear. State `clear` or `overlap` for each. Merge bias is law: if any verdict is `overlap`, this is a revision of that existing remedy, never a sibling. Set `overlap_action.revises` to that R token.

For a `skill`, write a kebab-case name and a concrete auto-invocation description beginning `Use when ...`; this description is the trigger. The body must be substantive Markdown. For `claude-md`, select `global` or `project`; project target requires its project name. For `hook`, give a Claude Code event and a command sketch. For `benchmark-only`, explain the measurement-only outcome in `note`.

The upstream classifier deliberately over-merges. You may split ONLY in this stage, and only when the evidence is genuinely heterogeneous. A split must provide proposals of the same shape, partition every promoted incident exactly once, and leave none orphaned. Otherwise return one proposal covering the group.

remedy_content.text:
## Honor Explicit Scope Constraints

When the user states an explicit constraint on what not to touch or how to proceed (e.g. "no network calls," "leave the formatter alone," "this patch must not touch tests"), treat it as a hard boundary for the rest of the task, not a one-time note. Do not modify the excluded resource, take the excluded action, or reintroduce it later in the same task even if it seems like the fastest path to a fix. If honoring the constraint appears to block progress, stop and ask the user how to proceed instead of silently overriding it.

structured_output.routing_rationale: All four promoted incidents (aurora #1, #3, #4; cinder #5) share one root cause: the agent violates an explicit, standing constraint the user already stated (no network calls, don't touch the formatter, don't touch tests) rather than treating it as a hard boundary for the rest of the task. There is nothing procedural or multi-step to teach here — no workflow, no tool sequence — so a skill would be overkill and would waste context budget. It also isn't mechanically enforceable: a hook can't know which files/actions a given free-text user instruction excludes, so there's no reliable PreToolUse gate to write. This is a pure instruction-following discipline gap, which is exactly what a short standing claude-md rule is for: remind the agent to hold explicit exclusions as durable constraints and to ask before overriding them rather than silently proceeding. Per merge bias, this is a revision of R3, broadening its wording to cover any explicit scope/action constraint, not just deletions.
